t: So Ben, big week in AI math. Actually, let me just say it straight: OpenAI dumped seven hundred and twenty-two manuscripts on GitHub this week, covering three hundred and seventy-two separate result groups. Each one claims to solve or seriously advance a major open problem in mathematics or theoretical computer science.

Three hundred and seventy-two. And these aren't homework problems. We're talking algebra, number theory, topology, mathematical logic, theoretical computer science. The kind of stuff that fields medals get handed out for.

Right, and the headline acts are wild. A claimed solution to the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture. Improvements to some genuinely important algorithms. And actual, concrete progress on the Riemann hypothesis.
The Riemann hypothesis! The million-dollar problem. People don't make progress on that, they tiptoe near it and publish a survey paper.
Okay, but before everyone loses their minds, here's the part that actually gives this credibility. A lot of these proofs have already been machine-verified in Lean.

For people who don't know Lean, it's a proof assistant. You translate the proof into this formal language and the computer checks every single logical step. If Lean says it compiles, the proof is correct. Full stop. No referee review needed on correctness.
So the results are almost certainly right. The open question is more interesting though: are they novel? Or did the model just remix existing techniques across three hundred seventy-two problems?

Exactly, and that's going to take mathematicians months to work out. OpenAI itself admits its own researchers haven't even digested most of these yet. They shipped the flood before anyone read the flood.

Now, context matters here, because this is a sequel. About a month ago, OpenAI claimed their internal model cracked Navier-Stokes. A Millennium Prize problem. One of the six biggest open problems in all of math.

And the way they did it was bonkers. A swarm of ten thousand AI agents working collectively, burning millions of dollars of compute. Whole saga was surrounded by controversy about how they released it.

Right, and that controversy got so bad that OpenAI put together an independent advisory group of mathematicians. Their guidelines said: if you release AI-generated results, publish the model, the exact prompt, and the compute time behind each result.
And this week? OpenAI published average compute time and some stats. No prompts. Model still unreleased. And their spokesperson said, quote, not bound by these recommendations.
But here's the claim that broke everyone's brain this time. The spokesperson said almost every one of these three hundred seventy-two results came from a single prompt, handed to a single AI agent.

Think about that contrast. Last month, one Millennium Prize problem needed a ten-thousand-strong swarm and millions of dollars. This month, three hundred seventy-two results from one agent, one prompt.
If that's true, it means the cost of frontier math is collapsing. From millions of dollars per problem to, what, a subscription fee?

If. That's doing a lot of work in that sentence. Andrew Sutherland at MIT put it perfectly: until the model is released and results can be replicated, treat any claim about one-shotting problems with a single agent as unverified. We should ask for receipts.
And the receipts situation is genuinely thin. OpenAI says the model is unreleased but they're, quote, working to release it as quickly and responsibly as possible. Which, sure.
Even Terence Tao weighed in. Arguably the best living mathematician. He called the pace of these frontier lab math dumps, his word, insane.

And there's a real debate buried in here. Some mathematicians, like Daniel Litt at Toronto, say look, if we want the answers to these questions, why would we ask the company to keep them secret? He thinks it's plainly good for mathematics.

Others say dumping hundreds of unexplained proofs on a community that can't absorb them, with no transparency about how they were made, is its own kind of chaos. One headline literally asked whether this counts as research misconduct.

So why is OpenAI even doing this? And the honest answer from the company is kind of telling. They said they can't slow down because hard math is the test that shows their AI really is getting smarter.
Which reframes the whole thing. These aren't love letters to mathematics. It's a benchmark race. Proof generation is the new eval.
But here's the angle I keep coming back to, the one that matters for people building with AI. Ignore the theorems for a second. Look at the trajectory.

Yeah. Last month, hardest problem in the world, needed ten thousand agents. This month, three hundred seventy-two problems, one agent, one prompt. Whatever is happening inside that unreleased model, the agentic capability curve just went vertical.

And if OpenAI releases that model, that's the real product story. Not the Kakeya conjecture. The fact that this level of sustained, verifiable reasoning might be something you or I could run against our own hard problems.
Formal verification is the quiet hero here too. Lean is what turns a suspicious claim into a checkable artifact. Verified output means the bottleneck shifts from is it right to is it useful.
So where does this land? The results are probably correct, the novelty is unproven, the transparency is incomplete, and the pace is only going up. That's the situation.

And months from now, when mathematicians finish parsing the pile, we'll know whether this was the week AI started doing real mathematics, or the week it learned to repackage the textbook very, very fast.
Either way, keep an eye on that repo. Links in the notes, and we'll catch you next time!
